This transcript was made from an earlier 46m version of the audio that has since been shortened to 21m. Some parts may not match playback.
Let's give it one minute. Okay, colleagues, I think I'll get started. Thanks for coming. It's been a quiet week here. As you saw, the process by which the Security Council recommends and the General Assembly appoints a new Secretary-General of the UN continues. The President remains committed to his impartial stewardship of this process, guided by the letter and the spirit of the UN Charter and relevant Assembly resolutions. This week, the President continued to fulfill his commitment to ensuring that formally nominated candidates have the opportunity to engage with the wider UN membership, including through his facilitation of an interactive dialogue with Ms. Lana Nuzeiba. He will continue to ensure equal treatment of all candidates, transparency, and appropriate opportunities for engagement with the wider membership. President remains equally committed to respecting the distinct responsibilities of the Security Council and the General Assembly under the Charter. Turning to the Assembly’s plenary work this week, on Monday the 26th, the Assembly met for its fifth annual debate on the use of the veto in the Security Council. President Rochman, in his opening remarks, noted that 21 meetings have now been held under the veto initiative, most recently on 1st October. He said that the veto initiative has become an established expression of transparency, accountability, and collective responsibility within our organization. He stressed that the effectiveness of the Security Council is not an abstract institutional matter. Instead, it has direct consequences for people living in conflict, insecurity, and with humanitarian suffering, and those people bear the cost when the Council is unable to act. And the President added, and I quote, "No veto should bring an end to dialogue and diplomacy." On Tuesday and Wednesday, the 27th and 28th of October, the plenary held its annual meeting on the agenda item entitled "Necessity of Ending the Economic, Commercial, and Financial Embargo Imposed by the United States of America Against Cuba." The President presided over the meetings. in accordance with the Assembly's Rules of Procedure, maintaining order and ensuring the delegations could exercise their procedural rights. On yesterday, on the 29th of October, the Assembly considered the annual report of the ICJ, the International Court of Justice, among several other agenda items. Today, the Assembly is convened for its annual debate on the report of the Human Rights Council. And on Monday, it will take up the report of the ICC. President Rachman also held several bilateral meetings this week, including with Monica Juma, Executive Director of UNODC; Amy Pope, the Director General of IOM; Mirjanus Boljaric, the President of the International Committee of the Red Cross; and Yuji Iwasawa, the President of the International Court of Justice. These engagements reflect the President's continued focus on peace and security, international law, humanitarian concerns, and the wider priorities of the General Assembly. So that's what we have on this week's big developments. I'll be happy to take your questions. There are no bad questions. Anyone online? Let me check. Okay, easy for me this week. Thank you, guys. Going once, going twice. Have a great weekend.
Greetings, Earthlings. Thank you. It's freezing in here.
As always, yes. It's a little dark too, no? No, isn't it darker than usual? Mark, can you press one of the lighting buttons? There you see? There you go, Mark. You wave your wand. All right, how's everybody today? It's Friday. Who's running the marathon? Anybody in the press corps running a marathon? No, our colleague Ignacio is running a marathon. Our former colleague Florencia is running the marathon. And one of our Kenyan colleagues from the SG security detail is running the marathon. Last year, he was the eighth or ninth Kenyon to come in, so we will report back on Monday. I am not running the marathon, in case there was a doubt in that in any way, shape, or form. After the marathon on Monday, and after my briefing on Monday, there'll be a briefing here by Ambassador Sanita Pavliuta-Deslandes, Permanent Representative of Latvia to the United Nations, and she'll be here because she will be the President of the Security Council for the month of November. She'll speak to you about the of work. That briefing will be in person only, so if you want to ask questions, be here, but you can also obviously follow on UN Web TV. Speaking of Security Council, this morning you will have seen that the Security Council unanimously adopted a draft resolution renewing the mandate of the UN Verification Mission until this October 31st, 2027. And as you recall, our mission in Colombia is a special political mission that was established in 2016. by the Security Council to verify the implementation of the final peace agreement and to support Colombia's efforts to end conflict and build sustainable peace. Turning to Ukraine, our colleague Tom Fletcher, the Emergency Relief Coordinator and Under Secretary General for Humanitarian Affairs, noted that each day the ceasefire in Oleshky holds means that hope for civilians in that city. He stressed that those wanting to leave must be able to do so safely and must be able to do so voluntarily. Let this pave the way for vital aid to get in, Mr. Fletcher said, as well as humanitarian access on both sides of the front line. Elsewhere in Ukraine, we, along with our humanitarian partners, are responding to the latest wave of deadly attacks on the regions of Chernihiv, Kharkiv, and Poltava. Aid organizations have been providing hot meals, cash assistance, emergency shelter assistance, and temporary repairs to the many damaged homes. Our colleagues on the ground also tell us that two humanitarian vehicles came under drone attack yesterday in the Zaporizhzhia region, a clearly marked bus was struck, killing a woman and injuring passengers and the driver. This bus service, which is supported by the Ukraine Humanitarian Fund, the UN's Ukraine Humanitarian Fund, provides essential transport to a community of more than 1,600 people. In the city of Sloviansk in Donetsk, an armored evacuation vehicle was hit, injuring two evacuees. Attacks against civilians, attacks against civilian infrastructure, And attacks targeting humanitarians are unacceptable and must stop, and they are contrary to international humanitarian law. Turning to Lebanon, our humanitarian colleagues on the ground tell us as of Wednesday, more than 300,000 men, women, and children remain internally displaced in the country. They have been displaced since March 2nd, and we are at the end of October, while nearly 970,000 people have been able to return to their communities in the southern part of Lebanon. Despite people's willingness to return to their homes, continued Israeli military activity and presence in southern Lebanon are undermining the Lebanese residents' ability to return safely and to be able to start rebuilding their lives. This week alone, further demolitions, fires, and strikes by Israeli defense forces were reported across the southern part of the country, both within the so-called combat zone declared by Israel, from which residents were ordered to evacuate, and beyond it, where communities were also affected by these actions. OCHA cautions that the humanitarian crisis is far from Over, many people returning find their homes damaged, essential services disrupted, and their livelihoods very challenging to try to start to resume. For those who returned, earning a living remains a major challenge. In Nabatieh Governorate, for example, insecurity and restrictions on access to agricultural land are disrupting the olive harvest there. In some villages, farmers have been able to harvest for only two days before being forced by Israeli army to stop doing so. As part of the humanitarian response, the Lebanon Humanitarian Fund has allocated $91 million to support displaced people, returnees, refugees, and other communities affected by this year's escalation. Without safety, without access to essential services, and without opportunities to earn a living, families cannot rebuild their lives. We reiterate our call for the protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure, unimpeded humanitarian access, and the facilitation by all parties of the safe and dignified return of people to their homes. Turning to Yemen, our OCHA colleagues there tell us that more than 290,000 people have now been forced from their homes since the beginning of August, as fighting shows no sign of abating. Pregnant women are among the most at risk. Our colleagues at the UN Population Fund tell us that nearly 6,100 pregnant women were among the most recently displaced, including 600 who are expected to give birth within the next two weeks. UNFPA has deployed mobile teams and midwives to help support them. They have been sent to displacement sites and delivered maternal health supplies to support the response. The crisis is also impacting refugees already living in Yemen, as you can imagine. UNHCR says more than 65,000 refugees and asylum seekers face a rapidly worsening humanitarian situation, with services disrupted and rising food and fuel prices making it harder for families to meet the most basic needs. Since August, UNHCR has helped more than 600 Somali refugees voluntarily return home from Yemen. Our humanitarian partners are scaling up their response where they can, and they've now supported nearly 249,000 displaced people, representing almost three in four of those displaced. And that support includes food, hygiene, and other and emergency cash. We reiterate on call here as well to for the parties to protect civilians, to protect civilian infrastructure, to respect international humanitarian law, and to allow for the safe and unimpeded delivery of humanitarian aid wherever it is needed and for for whoever it is for. Crossing the water to Eritrea, Tom Fletcher as well here, allocated $3.5 million from the UN Central Emergency Response Fund to support early action for impact of El Nino in that country. The strengthening El Nino is having a significant impact on the Horn of Africa, including in Eritrea, which is experiencing below average rainfall, affecting crop and livestock productivity, pasture regeneration, and the availability of water, which is essential for everything. These impacts are expected to worsen following the harvest and into the 2027 lean season. The new CERF allocation markets, districts most impacted by El Nino in Eritrea. The Food Agriculture Organization, for its part, joined by the UN Development Program, the UN Population Fund, and UNICEF, will all work closely with the government counterparts to assist people in priority areas through integrated interventions, addressing food security, livelihoods, nutrition, maternal and newborn health, and water and sanitation hygiene. The response will promote community ownership and build resilience to future climate shocks. Priority will go to children under the age of five, pregnant and nursing mothers, pastoral and agropastoral households, as well as households headed by women. And next door in Ethiopia, we, along with our partners, continue to reach people in need in the northern part of the country, despite the insecurity and criminal activity going on there that have delayed the movement of humanitarian supplies. In the Amhara region, the World Food Program is providing nutrition supplies to more than 254,000 moderately malnourished women and children this month. In Wagh Hamra zone, our humanitarian partners also continue to provide health, nutrition, water, sanitation, hygiene assistance, as well as protection services. In Tigray, our partners dispatched 13 food trucks yesterday to support more than 57,000 displaced people in four districts in the central zone. Our NGO dispatch medicine to two hospitals in the towns of Shire and Shiraro, benefiting more than 38,000 men, women, and children there. Despite these efforts, our humanitarian colleagues note that the assistance remains insufficient to meet the growing needs of the people. In the Amhara region, our humanitarian colleagues say that people who've recently returned to the districts of Abergel and Chakabji urgently need food, water, and essential aid. And a new influx of internally displaced people arriving in the region after fleeing escalating violence in the neighboring regions of Oromia and central Ethiopia, also putting pressure on an already overstretched humanitarian system. And in Afghanistan, also from our humanitarian colleagues, they tell us that renewed clashes near the Torkham border crossing with Pakistan are putting civilians, including aid workers, at risk. On Wednesday, a child from the local community was killed and a humanitarian worker assisting families returning from Pakistan also injured in the fighting. Despite the tensions, we and our humanitarian partners remain on the ground providing aid at the border and nearby reception and transit centers. Our humanitarian colleagues say that Torkham is a major crossing point for Afghans returning from Pakistan. More than 600,000 people have crossed there between January and the start of this month, accounting for Nearly 85% of people recorded as having returned from Pakistan. Previous escalations have forced the crossing to close, as you'll remember, and our humanitarian partners to relocate some services temporarily. We call on all parties to protect civilians, protect civilian infrastructure, and allow for the free and unhindered distribution of humanitarian aid. A quick note from our good friends at UNHCR, who today launched their annual winter fundraising appeal. UNHCR pointed out that facing funding shortfalls and surging energy prices, at least 9 million human beings are estimated to require additional assistance to get through this winter across four war-impacted countries: Ukraine, Syria, Lebanon, and Afghanistan. To help offset the deep decline in its budget, UNHCR is aiming to raise at least $50 million for winter support for the 2026-2027 winter, 3 million more than it raised last year through its annual campaign aimed at individual and private donors. Lastly, no money, but a bit of an International Day quiz. If you already know what International Day is coming up tomorrow, don't spoil it for your colleagues. Eridu, Uruk, and Tell Brak are three ancient sites that have something in common. They all claim to be-- have been given the same title. There are now, these sites are in southern Iraq and in Syria. According to the World History Encyclopedia, each one has been called the world's first city, which means that tomorrow is World City Day. Ah, Efraim, thank you for thinking. Even on a Friday. It is World Cities Day tomorrow. In his message, the Secretary-General says more than 3 billion people in cities do not have access to adequate housing, including 1.1 billion living in informal settlements. He says housing is more than just shelter. He's urging cities everywhere to invest in adequate housing for all. Ephraim, you may, you yield to, or Edie, I think he yields to you by default.
Thank you, Steph. Has the United Nations played any role at all in the evacuation of hundreds of people from Oleshky?
We have not, but we are there on the receiving end, providing humanitarian aid to people who have been evacuated.
And where is this aid being provided specifically?
On the Ukrainian side, people coming back into Ukraine. I can give you the exact location as soon as I get it.
Okay. Volodymyr, maybe you have the answer. No, go ahead.
Thank you, Stéphane. Yesterday during the briefing, the Russian strike on the railway station in Dnipro, Ukraine, was mentioned. The death toll has since risen to 15. A remotely operated drone was deliberately directed at the platform where people were waiting for a train. Does the Secretary General consider this attack involving the deliberate targeting of civilians for political purposes an act of terrorism?
The Secretary General strongly condemns the attack we saw on Dnipro. by the armed forces of the Russian Federation on Ukraine. As you mentioned, civilians were killed, including children. This is not an isolated case. It comes on the heels of attacks by the Russian Federation on Ukrainian cities, including Kyiv, Kharkiv, Odesa, and Zaporizhzhia. All of these attacks are violations of international humanitarian law, and they must stop. Abdelhamid, I see your hand with a microphone in your hand.
OK. There was an art exhibit in the curved wall near Vienna Cafe. It was opened on Tuesday evening. It disappeared on Wednesday morning. It is being mounted now again. So there must be something happened in the Secretariat who decided to put it.
Yeah, I mean, the exhibit, as you mentioned, is going back up. All exhibits at UN headquarters are organized in accordance with a standard procedure administering the use of space at UN headquarters. Part of that involves a review of the exhibit as installed. To put it in simple terms, there was an agreement on the exhibit and the wording. I think the exhibit that went up didn't match exactly what had been agreed to. There was further negotiations in a quick amount of time, and agreement was reached, and the exhibit is going back up, which is great. Ephraim, and then Murad.
Thank you, Steph. The Houthis have been suspected of using chemical weapons in the besieged city of Taiz, and the governor of the city has called on the UN to investigate. I wonder if you are following these reports. What is the Secretary General’s reaction on these initial reports?
We’re following these worrying reports. As you know, we do not have anybody on the ground in the city. We also, to be honest, and our partners that we work with, have neither the mandate nor the capacity to investigate these reports. But obviously, We'll continue to follow the situation closely, and if we have any more information, we will share it.
Do you have any granularity on the numbers you gave us of the displaced in Yemen? 290,000. Do we know if this includes the ones that are displaced inside Ta'z? And also those who have been reached by humanitarian workers, the 249,000. Are there part of it?
Yeah, I mean, that's the overall number of displaced people throughout that we've reported since August. I'll try to get you a bit more of a breakdown. What did I say? Morad, sorry.
A follow-up on Afram's question. Does the SCG support an independent investigation on this allegation?
Well, I mean, I think there are bodies within the UN, notably the OPCW, that are hold that mandate. Obviously, if there are repeated allegations of the use of chemical weapons, they need to be looked into. Abdelhamid, yes, and then I will go to our friend Joseph Klein, who's on line. Go ahead.
Yes. The two political blocs in Israel, one got 53, led by Netanyahu, and the other got 49, I think, by Yitzhak Rabin. Both parties are distancing themselves from the Arabs, who got 19 seats. Don't you see that as racism at its worst face?
Look, I'm not going to get involved in the rather complicated Israeli political negotiations following these elections. Mr. Klein? Joe? All right, no Joe. Pam.
Thank you, Steph. We've heard about all the troops in Haiti. Is there any first-hand information you're getting from the UN on what's happening, and is it...
The last round. the Salvador troops. Thank you.
I mean, I think we're aware of the reports about additional Salvador personnel, military personnel being deployed to Haiti. The vast majority of those, from what I understand, fall outside of the scope of the UN Support Office's mandate. As you know, the UN Support Office is there to support troops from the gang suppression force, logistical and operational support, and also on the applicable verification human rights due diligence mandate.
I'm sorry, as a follow-up, I'm just asking because we're getting just messages from people in Haiti that things are pretty desperate. Are you hearing?
Well, I mean, let's be honest, I think anybody who's been following this briefing knows that things are pretty desperate in Haiti. We've been trying to get that point across. We've been trying to give you the information to report on. I think there's no debate about the desperate situation that the Haitian people are currently under, given all the humanitarian challenges they have and given the continued violence, abhorrent and blind violence being perpetrated by criminal gangs. OK, on that note, Mr. Klein, I'll give you one more chance to unmute. Going once, twice. See you Monday.
